headline: NZ Parliament Mourns Nine Weather Deaths as Election-Year Cost-of-Living Clash Begins
summary: Parliament opened its 2026 session by approving a motion of condolence for people killed in landslides and flooding, while speakers also called for support for affected communities and stronger disaster resilience. The Prime Minister then promoted the Government’s economic and policy programme ahead of the November election, drawing sharp opposition challenges over living costs, jobs, public services and environmental policy. MPs also debated proposed education and justice changes, mental health services and legislation intended to make rules easier to find.

topicSummaries.topic: House Pays Tribute to Nine Weather-Related Deaths
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The landslides and floods killed people and left families, homes and local services affected across several North Island regions.
topicSummaries.content: The House approved Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s motion expressing condolences after recent severe weather events. Six people were presumed dead in the Mount Maunganui landslide, two died in a separate slip at Welcome Bay, and one person died in the flooded Mahurangi River; a man was still missing near Ōpōtiki. Luxon said Cabinet had approved recovery funding and that the Government would work with councils and communities. Labour leader Chris Hipkins supported the motion and urged the Government to give Tauranga City Council’s independent review of the Mount Maunganui landslide the full powers of a Government inquiry. Green and Te Pāti Māori speakers called for improved preparation and locally directed support, while ACT and NZ First speakers cautioned against drawing conclusions before investigations were complete. The motion was followed by a moment of silence.

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Our Government is committed to doing what is needed, working with councils and communities on the recovery and the rebuild.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: I would encourage the Government to give it the full powers of a Government inquiry so that it can have public support and public credibility.

topicSummaries.topic: Cost of Living and Recovery Claims Dominate Election-Year Debate
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Disagreement over prices, jobs and economic growth bears directly on household budgets and people’s ability to find work and remain in New Zealand.
topicSummaries.content: Luxon said the economic recovery had arrived, citing higher business confidence, growth in manufacturing and tourism, more building consents and rising exports, while acknowledging that many people had yet to feel the benefits. Labour leader Chris Hipkins disputed that assessment, pointing to weaker-than-forecast growth, higher-than-forecast debt and inflation at 3.1 percent, and arguing that food, power and housing costs were squeezing families. Other Labour MPs highlighted hardship withdrawals from KiwiSaver and people leaving the country; Finance Minister Nicola Willis defended the Government’s spending restraint and reforms, saying Labour had not set out credible alternatives. These were arguments made by MPs during the debate, rather than findings agreed by the House.

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I feel more confident than ever that the recovery has now arrived and that Kiwis can look forward to a year that is brighter than the last few have been

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The cost of living, far from getting better, has continued to get worse for Kiwi families.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Defends Crime Strategy as Opposition Challenges Results
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Police capacity, drug-related harm and youth offending affect community safety, businesses and victims of crime.
topicSummaries.content: Luxon cited Government figures showing 38,000 fewer victims of violent crime, youth offending down 16 percent and ram raids down 85 percent. Labour’s Ginny Andersen challenged the Government’s law-and-order record, saying it had not delivered its promised 500 additional police officers and citing a 97 percent rise in methamphetamine entering communities. She also criticised the Government’s retail-crime advisory group and military-style youth academies, arguing that prevention programmes initiated under Labour had contributed to falling ram raids. Children’s Minister Karen Chhour defended the Government’s approach as combining consequences with support for young people and families, and said military-style academies were among several interventions being trialled. The competing claims were not resolved in the debate.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ginny Andersen (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Well over 80 percent—as we know from the failed trial—reoffend in New Zealand.

topicSummaries.topic: Education Changes Face Questions Over Evidence and Consultation
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to classroom teaching, qualifications and school governance will affect students, teachers and families across the country.
topicSummaries.content: Luxon highlighted the Government’s literacy and numeracy programme, including daily instruction in reading, writing and maths, and reported that the share of new entrants meeting the expected phonics level had risen from 36 to 58 percent. He also reiterated plans to replace NCEA with a qualification using grades out of 100 and stronger vocational pathways. Green education spokesperson Lawrence Xu-Nan challenged the Government’s interpretation of its assessment results, arguing that the tests covered narrow skills and that different students had been tested at different points. Labour’s Willow-Jean Prime criticised changes to curriculum and school governance, alleging insufficient consultation with educators and concern about the Teaching Council’s independence. The Government presented its changes as a drive to improve achievement; opposition speakers questioned the evidence and process.

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The number of new entrants achieving where they should be in phonics has gone from 36 percent to 58 percent.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lawrence Xu-Nan (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Education depends on trust, nuance, professional scepticism, and long-term thinking—not slogans, not victory laps, not labels that have been used on something that is a narrow test within the whole pedagogical system.

topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Higher default contributions would direct more money into retirement savings and change the amount contributed from pay over time.
topicSummaries.content: As part of his 2026 programme, Luxon said default KiwiSaver contribution rates were due to rise from 3 percent to 3.5 percent later in the year. He said he hoped they would increase to 4 percent in 2028 and eventually to 6 percent if National were re-elected. Luxon argued that higher contributions would build retirement balances and provide more capital for investment in New Zealand businesses and infrastructure. The statement set out the Government’s intended direction; the later proposed increases were not legislative decisions made in the House that day.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Details India Trade Deal Covering 95% of Exports
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Lower tariffs could affect export opportunities and jobs in industries including agriculture, horticulture, wine and manufacturing.
topicSummaries.content: Trade Minister Todd McClay described the free-trade agreement with India, concluded before Christmas, as a significant opportunity for New Zealand exporters. He said it covered 95 percent of New Zealand exports, with 57 percent of goods exports becoming duty-free from the start and a larger share receiving duty-free access once the agreement was fully in force. McClay said the deal also allowed up to 1,670 skilled workers from India to work in New Zealand each year for three years, with participation limited to skills the economy needs and workers required to return home. He said he would discuss the agreement with the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee before bringing it to the House later in the year.

topicSummaries.topic: Mental Health Minister Reports Faster Access and New Response Teams
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Timely access to mental health support can reduce delays for people in crisis and improve access to care in communities.
topicSummaries.content: Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey said more than 11 percent additional frontline mental health workers had been added since the Government took office, and reported that 83.4 percent of people seeking primary mental health support were seen within a week. He also said 82.2 percent of people awaiting specialist mental health care were seen within three weeks, and that people brought to emergency departments under a police mental health change programme were now handed over within an hour. Doocey announced four new locations for mental health co-response teams pairing clinicians with police, as part of a $28 million programme. These figures and assessments were presented by the Minister during the debate.

topicSummaries.topic: Legislation Bill Prompts Dispute Over Scrutiny of Rule Changes
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill aims to make rules affecting the public easier to locate, while its proposed revision process raises questions about parliamentary oversight.
topicSummaries.content: Attorney-General Judith Collins moved the Legislation Amendment Bill’s second reading, saying it would require agencies to publish secondary legislation and related information, helping turn the New Zealand Legislation website into a central access point. Labour speakers supported the access measures, while the Greens said they could not support the bill as drafted because changes expanding the scope of revision bills might reduce scrutiny; they also raised concerns about a further amendment paper that Collins said she intended to release. Labour MP Duncan Webb likewise warned that revision bills should not be used to change the substance of laws. The second-reading debate was interrupted and set down to resume the next sitting day; the House had not completed the bill’s passage.

keyExchanges.speaker: Judith Collins (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Everything will be identified, indexed, and linked, and it will, over time, turn the New Zealand Legislation website into what it should be: a one-stop shop for legislation and information about that legislation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lawrence Xu-Nan (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: The Green Party cannot support this bill, currently.

conclusion: The House united in mourning those killed by the severe weather, but its opening debate of election year exposed unresolved divisions over whether the Government’s recovery is reaching households and how economic growth should be balanced with public services, environmental protection and accountability.
